295.title: Philosophy for women too
295.hook: Musonius Rufus argued women should study philosophy as men do (Musonius Rufus, Lecture 3)
295.howItsDone: Stoicism today is practiced by people of every background, and many point to Musonius Rufus's lectures as an early argument that philosophy belongs to all.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the citadel, the mind free from runaway passions. Your line was the citadel. Where did you find your minute of quiet? Day two hundred ninety-five.

Rome, the first century. A girl learns to spin wool, run a household, keep accounts, and marry well. Her brother, if the family has money, learns rhetoric and philosophy. Nobody thinks to question it; it's simply how things are. Then a Stoic teacher stands up in front of his students and questions it. Not in a whisper. As a lecture, with arguments, one after another. His name was Musonius Rufus, and you've met his most famous student without knowing it. This week, the Stoics honestly. Today: philosophy for women too.
screen: `ROME, THE FIRST CENTURY.` → `SPINNING FOR HER, BOOKS FOR HIM.` → `A TEACHER QUESTIONS IT.`

segments.voice: Musonius Rufus was a Roman Stoic who taught in Greek, was sent into exile more than once by emperors who found him inconvenient, and taught a young man named Epictetus. We have his lectures because a student wrote them down and a later collector, Stobaeus, preserved them. The third lecture asks whether women should study philosophy, and his answer is yes. His arguments are simple and sharp. Women have received from the gods the same power of reason as men. They have the same senses: sight, hearing, touch. They have the same natural desire for goodness, and they're just as pleased by fine and just actions. So why should it be fitting for men to seek how to live well, and not for women? In the next lecture he goes further: daughters should be educated the same way as sons, because the virtues, courage, justice, self-control, wisdom, are the same for everyone. Now the honesty this week promises. Musonius still pictured most women running households, and he thought some tasks suit men and some suit women. He wasn't arguing for everything we'd argue for today. But he did say the one thing that mattered most to a Stoic, virtue, belongs equally to both. And he wasn't alone in the neighborhood. Hipparchia, the Cynic philosopher, married Crates, dressed like him, argued in public and was remembered for it. So in a school that says the only true good is character, the door to philosophy was, at least in principle, open to everyone with a mind. Philosophy for everyone.

296.title: Slave and emperor
296.hook: Epictetus enslaved, Marcus on the throne: one school, very different lives
296.howItsDone: Readers of Stoicism often study Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius side by side, and reflect on playing well the role life has handed them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Musonius Rufus and philosophy for women too. Your line was philosophy for everyone. Who did you share an idea with? Day two hundred ninety-six.

Two men. One was born around the year fifty in a town in what's now Turkey, into slavery. He was owned, sold, sent where he was told. He walked with a limp for most of his life. The other was born seventy years later into one of the richest families in Rome, was picked as a boy for the throne, and became the most powerful person in the known world. It's hard to imagine two lives further apart. And yet the second man learned how to live from the first one's words. Today: slave and emperor.
screen: `ONE BORN INTO SLAVERY.` → `ONE PICKED FOR THE THRONE.` → `SLAVE AND EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: The first man is Epictetus. Even his name carries his story: in Greek it means acquired, the kind of word you'd use for property. His owner, Epaphroditus, served at the court of Nero, and somehow the enslaved young man was allowed to attend the lectures of Musonius Rufus, the teacher we met yesterday. Later he was freed. He taught in Rome until the emperor Domitian banished the philosophers, then opened a school in Nicopolis in Greece. He never wrote a book. A student named Arrian wrote down his talks, and that's the Discourses and the Handbook we've been quoting all year. The second man is Marcus Aurelius. At the start of his Meditations he thanks the people who formed him, and one of them is his tutor Rusticus, for introducing him to the discourses of Epictetus and lending him his own copy. So the emperor learned freedom from the notes of a former slave. Here's what's striking. They teach the same thing. What's up to us is our own judgment and choice, and nothing else. Epictetus has an image for it in his Handbook: you're an actor in a play, and the author gives out the parts. Maybe a poor man, maybe a ruler, maybe someone who's lame. Your job is to play the part well; choosing it isn't yours. Coming from a man who was handed slavery, that's not a slogan. And coming from a man handed an empire, it's a warning not to confuse the costume with the person. One school. Two very different parts. The same work.

segments.voice: Think about the part you were handed. Not chosen: handed. The family, the body, the place and time you were born, the money or lack of it. Just notice it, without judging whether it's fair. Then ask quietly: within this part, what's mine to play well today? Rest with that question. The bell holds the time.
Slave and emperor. Epictetus, born enslaved, and Marcus Aurelius, who ruled Rome: one school, very different lives, the same teaching. Today's word.

297.title: Where they fell short
297.hook: the Stoics lived with slavery and empire, and admiring them doesn't mean agreeing with everything
297.howItsDone: Many modern readers of the Stoics keep their practical teachings while openly acknowledging the Stoics' acceptance of slavery and their entanglement with wealth and imperial power.

segments.voice: Yesterday: slave and emperor, Epictetus and Marcus. Your line was the same school. What part were you handed, and what's yours to play? Day two hundred ninety-seven.

Everybody has had a hero who turned out to be a person. A coach, a grandparent, a musician whose songs got you through a hard year, and then one day you learn something about them that doesn't fit. What do you do with that? Throw them out entirely? Pretend you didn't hear it? There's a third way, and this path has been quoting the Stoics for most of a year, so we owe it to them, and to you, to try it here. Today: where they fell short.
screen: `A HERO WHO TURNED OUT TO BE A PERSON.` → `THROW OUT, OR PRETEND?` → `A THIRD WAY.`

segments.voice: Start with slavery. The Stoics said all humans share the same reason, that we're citizens of one world, that a slave's mind is as free as an emperor's. And they lived in a society built on slavery, and never, as far as we know, called for ending it. Seneca wrote a famous letter telling his friend to treat enslaved people as human beings: eat with them, speak kindly, remember that fortune could swap your places. That's real, and it was more than many Romans said. But Seneca himself owned many people, and the letter asks for kinder masters, not for no masters. Then wealth and power. Seneca was enormously rich while writing about the simple life, and he served as adviser to Nero. When Nero had his own mother killed, the historian Tacitus reports that Seneca was believed to have written the letter explaining it to the Senate. Marcus Aurelius spent much of his reign at war, and Christians were put to death in parts of the empire while he ruled; historians still debate how much he knew or directed. So what do we do? The Stoics themselves give us the tool. Epictetus said no one is a finished sage; everyone is making progress, or not. They never claimed to be perfect. Admiring them honestly means keeping the teaching that holds, the dichotomy of control, the circles, the citadel, and naming plainly where they didn't live up to their own best ideas. Which raises the uncomfortable question. What will people three hundred years from now say we couldn't see?

segments.voice: Let yourself wonder about our own time. What do almost all of us accept, the way Romans accepted slavery, that people later might find hard to believe? You don't need a perfect answer. Just let one candidate come up. Hold it without defending yourself or beating yourself up. Only notice. The bell holds the time.
Where they fell short. The Stoics taught one shared humanity while living with slavery, wealth and empire: admire them honestly, not blindly. Today's word.

298.title: Not a stiff upper lip
298.hook: in English "stoic" means unfeeling, which isn't what the Stoics meant
298.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners today distinguish apatheia, freedom from runaway passions, from apathy, and allow grief and love their honest place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where they fell short, the Stoics and slavery, wealth and empire. Your line was honest admiration. What blind spot of our time came to mind? Day two hundred ninety-eight.

Read any sports page and you'll find it. The coach remained stoic after the loss. The widow was stoic at the funeral. In everyday English, stoic means jaw set, no tears, feelings locked in a box. Stiff upper lip. And people who've never read a word of Seneca think that's the whole philosophy: don't feel, or at least don't show it. After more than two weeks on the porch, you already know that's off. Today we look at how far off, and at a young emperor who cried. Today: not a stiff upper lip.
screen: `THE COACH REMAINED STOIC.` → `JAW SET, NO TEARS.` → `NOT A STIFF UPPER LIP.`

segments.voice: The confusion has a source. The Stoics' ideal was apatheia, freedom from pathos, the runaway passions we met two weeks ago. English turned that word into apathy, not caring at all, and turned stoic into unfeeling. But remember the actual teaching: the goal was freedom from feelings built on false judgments, and room for good ones, joy, wise wishing, caution. Epictetus said it directly in his Discourses: a person shouldn't be unfeeling like a statue, but should keep up his natural relationships, as a son, a brother, a father, a citizen. A statue feels nothing. A Stoic loves his family. Then there's grief. Seneca wrote a letter to a friend who had lost someone, and his advice was roughly this: let the eyes not be dry, and don't let them flood either; you may weep, just don't wail without end. And then, in the same letter, he confesses that when his own dear friend Annaeus Serenus died, he wept so much that he stands as an example of someone overcome by grief. That's a Stoic admitting it, in writing. And there's a story, from a late and not very reliable Roman history, that when young Marcus Aurelius wept at the death of his tutor, courtiers tried to stop him. The emperor Antoninus said, roughly: let him be human; neither philosophy nor empire takes away natural feeling. Whether or not it happened just that way, it's how later Romans remembered him. So the real Stoic is not the one with no tears. It's the one whose tears are honest, and who isn't swept away by them.
screen: `APATHEIA IS NOT APATHY.` · `NOT UNFEELING LIKE A STATUE.` · `SENECA WEPT FOR HIS FRIEND.` · `LET HIM BE HUMAN.` · then, large: `NOT UNFEELING.`

segments.voice: Find one feeling that's actually here right now. Tiredness, sadness, hope, relief, anything. Name it quietly. Now, instead of managing it, let it be felt fully, the way you'd let a wave reach the shore. Where is it in your body? How big is it, really? Stay with it, breathing, not pushing and not feeding it. The bell holds the time.
Not a stiff upper lip. The Stoics wanted freedom from runaway passions, not from feeling: honest tears, and a steady center. Today's word.
screen: `NOT A STIFF UPPER LIP — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not unfeeling. Today, feel one feeling fully, and if someone asks how you are, give them a true answer. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

299.title: Plain food, hard ground
299.hook: Musonius taught plain food and hard work as training (Musonius Rufus, Lectures 18–19)
299.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners keep simple meals and occasional small hardships, like a cold shower or a plain lunch, as training in contentment rather than as punishment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: not a stiff upper lip. The Stoics weren't unfeeling. Your line was not unfeeling. Did you let one feeling be felt? Day two hundred ninety-nine.
screen: `NOT A STIFF UPPER LIP — NOT UNFEELING.`

segments.voice: Think about how many decisions your food takes. What to order. Which of the forty cereals. Whether the coffee has the right milk. Delivery or pickup. We've built a world where the next small pleasure is always one tap away, and a lot of us feel a little worse for it, not better. Nearly two thousand years ago, a Roman teacher looked at the banquets of his city, the peacocks and the imported fish and the feasts that went on for hours, and gave his students some unfashionable advice. Today: plain food.
screen: `FORTY KINDS OF CEREAL.` → `ONE TAP AWAY.` → `PLAIN FOOD.`

segments.voice: That teacher was Musonius Rufus, whom we met four days ago arguing that women should study philosophy. Two of his lectures are about food, and he says something that sounds too simple: self-control at the table is the beginning and the foundation of self-control everywhere else. Why food? Because it comes around two or three times a day. It's the most frequent test you get. His advice is concrete. Prefer food that is cheap and easy to find: grains, vegetables, fruit, cheese, milk, honey. Eat to nourish the body, not to chase the next flavor. He repeats an old saying often credited to Socrates: most people live to eat, but a good person eats to live. In another lecture he turns to clothing and houses. Clothes are for protecting the body, not for showing off. A house is for shelter from heat and cold, not for being admired. And in a lecture on training, he says a person should get used to cold and heat, thirst and hunger, a hard bed and plain meals, not as punishment, but as practice. The Greek word is askēsis, training, the word athletes used. It's where English gets ascetic. That's the key. For Musonius, plain food isn't about being miserable, or about saving money, or about looking virtuous. It's a gym. Each simple meal is a small rep that makes you less easy to push around by wanting. Someone who's content with bread and cheese is harder to bribe, easier to please, and freer. Plain is training.
screen: `SELF-CONTROL STARTS AT THE TABLE.` · `CHEAP, SIMPLE, EASY TO FIND.` · `EAT TO LIVE.` · `ASKĒSIS: TRAINING, LIKE AN ATHLETE.` · then, large: `PLAIN IS TRAINING.`

segments.voice: If you have water nearby, take one slow sip. If not, just swallow and notice. Taste it: nothing fancy, and yet it's exactly what the body wants. Now picture a plain meal, bread, rice, an apple, whatever is simple where you live. Imagine eating it slowly, with no screen, no sauce, just the food. Notice any part of you that protests. That's the muscle. The bell holds the time.
Plain food. Musonius Rufus's training: simple meals and a little hardship, practiced so wanting has less hold on you. Today's word.
Your line: plain is training. Eat one plain meal today, slowly, and notice what you miss and what you don't. If you have any medical diet, keep to it. Day two hundred ninety-nine.

300.title: Is this what I feared?
300.hook: Seneca: set aside days to live on very little and ask if this is what you dreaded (Letters 18)
300.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners set aside occasional days of voluntary discomfort, like simple food or skipping a convenience, to see that what they fear losing is survivable.

segments.voice: Yesterday: plain food, Musonius's training. Your line was plain is training. What did you miss, and what didn't you? Day three hundred.

Day three hundred. Worth a breath of its own. Now think about the fear that sits in the back of a lot of minds: what if it all went away? The job, the savings, the comfortable apartment. What if I ended up with almost nothing? For most of us that fear never gets looked at directly. It just hums, and it shapes choices. Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius in the middle of a noisy Roman holiday, suggested an experiment. Not thinking about the fear. Trying it, on purpose, for a few days. Today: is this what I feared?
screen: `DAY THREE HUNDRED.` → `WHAT IF IT ALL WENT AWAY?` → `TRY IT ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: It's December in Rome, the festival of Saturnalia. The whole city is feasting, and Seneca writes that Rome is sweating with it. In the middle of this he writes his eighteenth letter. His advice: set aside a certain number of days, and live on the scantiest, cheapest food, in rough, coarse clothing. And while you do, ask yourself one question. In Richard Gummere's translation of 1917: "Is this the condition that I feared?" He gives the reason with a picture everyone in Rome would know. Soldiers practice maneuvers in peacetime, digging trenches with no enemy in sight, so that they won't panic when the real day comes. The soul should do the same in good times: train, while fortune is kind, for the day fortune isn't. And he's clear it shouldn't be a show, like rich Romans who played at poverty in fancy little rooms. Make the bed really hard and the bread really coarse. Here's a lovely detail. In the same letter Seneca quotes Epicurus, the founder of a rival school, who kept certain days of eating very little to see whether he was missing any real pleasure. Seneca borrows good ideas from wherever he finds them, and says so. What people usually discover, then and now, is surprising. The thing we dreaded turns out to be survivable, even ordinary. Plain bread is still bread. A cold room is still a room. And the fear that used to hum in the background gets quieter, because you've looked at it. You don't have to lose everything. You just have to find out you'd still be you.
screen: `SATURNALIA: ROME IS FEASTING.` · `LIVE ON VERY LITTLE FOR A FEW DAYS.` · `SOLDIERS DRILL IN PEACETIME.` · `SENECA QUOTES EPICURUS.` · then, large: `IS THIS WHAT I FEARED?`

segments.voice: Pick one comfort you'll go without today. Something small but real: the second coffee, the phone at lunch, the car for a short trip, the soft chair. Now, sitting here, imagine the moment you miss it. Let the little pang come. Then ask Seneca's question gently: is this what I feared? Stay with whatever answer comes. The bell holds the time.

301.title: The Stoic day
301.hook: morning preview, attention through the day, evening review
301.howItsDone: Many modern Stoics keep a short morning reflection, check in with themselves during the day, and write or think through an evening review before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Seneca's question, is this what I feared? Your line was the question itself. Which comfort did you go without, and what did you find? Day three hundred one.

Three weeks on the porch. We've looked at what the Stoics called good, how they saw feelings, their picture of the world, and, this week, the Stoics honestly: Musonius arguing for women's education, a slave and an emperor in the same school, where they fell short, their real tears, plain food, and Seneca's question. Big ideas, all of them. But a philosophy that lives only in your head is a hobby. The Stoics wanted it in your calendar, from waking to sleep. So today, before we turn to the science, we put it all into one ordinary day.
screen: `THREE WEEKS ON THE PORCH.` → `A PHILOSOPHY IN YOUR HEAD IS A HOBBY.` → `ONE ORDINARY DAY.`

segments.voice: The Stoic day has three parts, and you've met each one already on this path. First, the morning preview. Marcus Aurelius starts book two of his notebook this way, in George Long's translation: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial." It sounds grim, but he goes on: they act this way because they don't know good from bad, and they're my kin, so I can't be harmed by them or angry with them. It's a weather forecast for people, so the storm doesn't surprise you. Second, attention through the day. Epictetus has a whole talk on it. The Greek word is prosochē, attention, paying heed. His warning is practical: if you let your attention slip for a moment, don't imagine you'll pick it up again whenever you like. Carelessness today makes tomorrow's carelessness easier. So through the day, the Stoic keeps checking: is this up to me? What am I telling myself? Is this the jolt, or the yes? Third, the evening review. Seneca describes how his teacher Sextius, every night before sleep, questioned himself: what bad habit did I cure today? What fault did I resist? In what way am I better? Seneca says he does the same, when the lamp is out and his wife has fallen silent, and then he forgives himself and resolves to do better. Morning, you prepare. Daytime, you notice. Evening, you look back kindly and learn. None of it takes long. Together they make a whole day into practice.
screen: `MORNING: THE PREVIEW.` · `DAYTIME: PROSOCHĒ, ATTENTION.` · `EVENING: THE REVIEW.` · `PREPARE, NOTICE, LOOK BACK KINDLY.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE DAY.`

segments.voice: Let's do a small version of all three now. Preview: picture the next few hours. Who might test your patience? Meet them kindly in advance. Attention: now come right here, to this breath, and this one. Review: think back over the morning so far. One thing that went well. One thing to do better. Forgive it, and rest. The bell holds the time.
The Stoic day. A morning preview, attention through the day, and an evening review: the whole philosophy in one ordinary day. Today's word.

Your line: the whole day. Live one whole Stoic day, starting now: a check-in at lunch, and three questions tonight. That's our weeks on the porch. Next, the science of practice. Day three hundred one.

Seneca's evening review ends with forgiving himself
he looks back honestly, then forgives and resolves to do better.

fork.setup: it's the end of a Stoic day, the lamp is out. what does Seneca do?
options: review the day, then forgive himself.
fork.reveal: following his teacher Sextius, he asks what he cured, resisted and improved, then forgives and resolves to do better.

original.note: Greek: attention, paying heed; Epictetus's word for the Stoic's daytime practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoicism is a set of ideas.
what it means: a way to spend a whole day: preview, attention, review.
what a scholar hears: Meditations 2.1, Epictetus's Discourses 4.12 on prosochē, and Seneca's On Anger 3.36.
